craft:Do this one.name: Courrieu pipe workshop, Cogolin
craft:Do this one.teaser: Six generations have carved briar root from the Maures into pipes on the same Cogolin avenue since 1802
craft:Do this one.story: Cogolin is a pipe town because of the hills behind it: the tree heather of the Massif des Maures grows a dense root burl, the briar, that will take a flame without burning through. The Courrieu family has worked it here since 1802, six generations by their own count, and every pipe still leaves the workshop signed and stamped with a small silver rooster. It holds the state's Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant label. The free hour-long visit follows the wood from the uprooted burl to the polished bowl. Honest limit: it is a visit, not a class; no craft on the gulf takes students.
craft:Do this one.why: Ask to see a raw briar burl next to a finished bowl: the grain you buy is the root you saw.
facts: Watch the pipe-makers at work on a guided tour of the workshop, from raw briar to finished pipe, then the shop
Call 04 94 54 63 82; visits listed all year, workshop closes 18:00 and the shop keeps a midday break, but listings differ on days, so call first (Oct 2026)

craft:Other one.name: Rigotti reed works, Cogolin
craft:Other one.teaser: Saxophone reeds cut from cane grown beside the Cogolin plain, almost all of them shipped abroad
craft:Other one.story: Since 1966 the Rigotti family has grown the giant cane of the Cogolin plain and shaped it into reeds for saxophone and clarinet. Franco Rigotti founded the works; his son Daniel runs it now, and about 95 percent of what leaves the route de la Mole is exported to players in the United States, Japan and Europe. The tourist office's guided tour walks you from the cane field to the sliver of reed that sits under a player's lip. Missing: an open door. You can only go in on the few dates the tourist office schedules each year, and there is no class.
craft:Other one.why: The 28 October 2026 tour is the last listed this year; book it before the cane is cut again.
facts: Guided tour of the reed works, from growing the cane to cutting the reed
EUR 5 a person, groups of 4 to 15 (Oct 2026)
Through the Cogolin tourist office or amusezvous.net; 2026 dates listed 29 Jul, 23 Sep and 28 Oct, no visits otherwise

craft:Other two.name: La Manufacture, Cogolin
craft:Other two.teaser: Carpets still woven on Jacquard handlooms from the 1880s, in a small town better known for pipes
craft:Other two.story: On boulevard Louis Blanc, La Manufacture Cogolin weaves carpets on handlooms fitted with Jacquard mechanisms that date from the 1880s, the punched-card system that lets a weaver repeat a pattern thread for thread. The rugs go to hotels, yachts and private houses, and the old looms are the whole point of the place. Visitors are another matter: the day-to-day welcome is to the showroom, by appointment and on weekdays only, and visitor reviews complain of patchy hours. Missing: the looms. Outside the free guided tours on the European Heritage Days in September, you see the finished carpets, not the weaving.
craft:Other two.why: Ask in the showroom to see the pattern cards and samples; next September, book the Heritage Days tour.
facts: Showroom visit by appointment; loom-side tours only on the European Heritage Days (19 Sep in 2026, free, groups of up to 20)
Not stated; allow under an hour for the showroom

craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.name: What is sold as Provençal craft
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.teaser: The soap stamped Marseille and the lavender sachet may have come from much further than the stall
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.story: The seafront souvenir shops sell two things above all as Provence in a bag: soap stamped 'savon de Marseille' and lavender. Neither name guarantees where it came from. Savon de Marseille has no protected definition in law; the traditional recipe is about 72 percent vegetable oil with no animal fat, perfume or colouring, yet bars carrying the stamp are made in Asia, sometimes from tallow. Lavender is similar. Bulgaria, not France, is now the world's largest producer of lavender oil, and sachets and soaps sold on Provençal stalls may hold lavandin, the coarser hybrid, or synthetic scent.
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.why: Read the back of the packet, not the front: ingredients and origin tell you what the stamp does not.
facts: Turn the soap over: look for vegetable oils only (olive first), no tallow ('sodium tallowate'), and a maker's town; on lavender look for 'lavande fine' or the AOP Huile essentielle de lavande de Haute-Provence
Spend the money on something made in front of you: a Courrieu briar pipe or a Rigotti reed in Cogolin, or the chestnut goods of Collobrières (both have their own cards)

linger:RAWr Torréfaction.name: RAWr Torréfaction, Cogolin
linger:RAWr Torréfaction.teaser: A drum roaster in a Cogolin shopping arcade, and the gulf's best case for coffee as a craft
linger:RAWr Torréfaction.story: RAWr is a small roasting workshop in the Galerie Raimu on Cogolin's main avenue, twenty minutes inland from Cavalaire. The green beans arrive from origin and are roasted on site, so on a roasting morning the arcade smells of toasting grain before you reach the door. Behind the counter they brew their own single origins, and the shelves carry the beans by the bag, brewing kit, organic teas and matcha, with a few homemade pastries. It is the nearest the gulf comes to a third-wave coffee bar, and the dog is welcome too.
linger:RAWr Torréfaction.why: Ask what came off the roaster this week and buy a bag of it, ground for the boat's machine.

Brunch runs all morning, there is a 20-seat terrace, and you can take a cup away. It opens early, which suits a crew coming off a mooring before the heat.

linger:Soeurs Coffee & Bakery.teaser: Cavalaire has no roaster of its own; this is where you get a decent flat white and a croissant
linger:Soeurs Coffee & Bakery.story: Be clear about what Cavalaire offers: no roaster, no specialty bar. Soeurs, on avenue Pierre Rameil in the town centre, is the honest best of the in-town options, a bakery, coffee shop and brunch room run by Matthieu and Valentin, with artisan ice cream in the counter as well. It is open every day of the year, which counts for a lot in a resort that thins out from October. Come for a flat white and a viennoiserie still warm from the oven, not for single-origin talk; for that, drive to RAWr in Cogolin.

drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.name: Côtes de Provence rosé
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.teaser: Pale by design and dry to the last drop: the bottle on nearly every table round the bay
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.story: The paleness is a choice made in the cellar. Côtes de Provence rosé is pressed straight from the grape, or left on the skins for only a few hours, then fermented cold, so the juice takes the faintest onion-skin tint while the wine stays dry. It is the great appellation of the region, and rosé makes up close to nine bottles in ten of what it produces. Around the bay the vines grow within sight of the sea, and the better bottles finish with a salty edge. It does not keep: the newest vintage is the one to drink, cold, this year.
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.why: Order the youngest vintage on the list and send back anything served warm.
facts: Pale pink; red currant, citrus peel, a dry, faintly saline finish
Côtes de Provence AOC and the most recent vintage

Un rosé de l'année, bien frais. Names close to Cavalaire: Domaine de la Croix and Domaine de la Bastide Blanche (La Croix-Valmer), Château Minuty (Gassin), Domaine La Tourraque (Ramatuelle). For darker, longer-lived rosé, Bandol, west of Toulon: the Var guide covers it

drink:Cru Classé rosé.name: Cru Classé rosé
drink:Cru Classé rosé.teaser: Provence ranked its own estates in 1955; eighteen still print 'Cru Classé', two of them close by
drink:Cru Classé rosé.story: In 1955 a ministerial decree classified a set of Côtes de Provence estates as crus classés, decades before the appellation itself existed. Of that list, eighteen still use the words on their labels, and two are within half an hour of Cavalaire: Domaine de la Croix above La Croix-Valmer and Château Minuty at Gassin. The rank was given on reputation and standing at the time, not after a blind tasting, and it has never been revised. A Cru Classé rosé usually has more grip and density than the house pink, and costs more.
drink:Cru Classé rosé.why: Taste one Cru Classé next to a plain Côtes de Provence from the same village and judge the gap yourself.
facts: Pale, but fuller and firmer than the house pink; more length
'Cru Classé' printed under Côtes de Provence AOC, with the estate name
Un rosé cru classé. Names: Domaine de la Croix (La Croix-Valmer), Château Minuty (Gassin); both have their own cards in the larder

drink:Tibouren.name: Tibouren
drink:Tibouren.teaser: The peninsula's own grape gives a rosé that smells of hot pine and salt, not boiled sweets
drink:Tibouren.story: Tibouren is the old grape of this stretch of coast, long planted around Saint-Tropez and now rare elsewhere. It makes a savoury rosé with a faint orange cast, smelling of garrigue herbs rather than strawberries. The place to taste it is the sandy strip between Cap Lardier and Cap Taillat, where Bastide Blanche's vines run almost to the cliff path and the wind off the sea scours them. Bastide Blanche shares its owners with Domaine de la Croix, so treat the two as one house, not rivals. Both it and La Tourraque, inside the three-capes site at Ramatuelle, are certified organic.
drink:Tibouren.why: Drink a Tibouren rosé beside a supermarket Provence and you will taste what 'saline' means.
facts: Pale with an orange tint; garrigue, dried herbs, pine resin, a salty finish
Côtes de Provence AOC, with Tibouren named on the back label or the cuvée
Un rosé à base de Tibouren. Names: Domaine de la Bastide Blanche (La Croix-Valmer), Domaine La Tourraque (Ramatuelle)

drink:Rolle, the white.name: Rolle, the white
drink:Rolle, the white.teaser: Vermentino under its Provençal name: citrus pith and sea spray, and rarely sold outside the region
drink:Rolle, the white.story: Rolle is what Provence calls Vermentino, the grape that also makes the whites of Corsica and Liguria. Near this coast it gives a white with the bitterness of citrus pith and a mineral, sea-spray finish, and it is the wine for the morning catch from the fishermen's quay, grilled or raw. Provence makes far less white than rosé, and most of it is drunk here, so a good bottle of Rolle is easier to find on a village shelf than on a wine list abroad.
drink:Rolle, the white.why: Buy a bottle of local Rolle for the boat; you will struggle to find the same one at home.
facts: Pale gold; lemon pith, white flowers, a bitter-almond, salty finish
Côtes de Provence blanc; Rolle or Vermentino on the back label
Un blanc de Rolle. Names: Domaine de la Croix (La Croix-Valmer), Domaine La Tourraque (Ramatuelle)

drink:The red for a cool evening.name: The red for a cool evening
drink:The red for a cool evening.teaser: Provence is not only pink: Mourvèdre and Syrah for the night the mistral turns the deck cold
drink:The red for a cool evening.story: Most visitors leave Provence without opening a red, and miss the wine for an October night. Mourvèdre and Syrah on the warmer soils give a dark red that smells of herbs, black olive and leather, built for lamb, daube or a grilled steak after the wind has cleared the sky. The one fix most people need is the temperature: serve it lightly cool, around 15°C, not at the heat of a summer cabin, which makes these reds taste of alcohol.
drink:The red for a cool evening.why: Put the bottle in the fridge for twenty minutes before dinner.
facts: Deep red; black fruit, garrigue herbs, black olive, leather
Côtes de Provence rouge; Mourvèdre and Syrah in the blend
Un rouge de Provence, légèrement frais. Names: Domaine de la Croix (La Croix-Valmer), Domaine La Tourraque (Ramatuelle); for the long-keeping Mourvèdre reds, Bandol, in the Var guide

drink:Pastis.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis.teaser: One measure, five of cold water, and the glass turns cloudy: the coast's apéritif, distilled in the hills
drink:Pastis.story: The ritual does not change: a measure of pastis, about five of cold water poured over it, then ice, and the clear spirit turns milky yellow, the 'louche'. It is drunk in the shade before lunch or at six in the evening. Most bars pour Ricard or Pastis 51, both from Marseille. Henri Bardouin is the one to ask for: Distilleries et Domaines de Provence blend it from more than 65 plants and spices, where the big brands lean on anise and liquorice. It is made inland at Forcalquier, in Haute-Provence. The coast owns the ritual; the hills make the bottle.
drink:Pastis.why: Ask for a Bardouin and add the water yourself from the carafe, ice last.
facts: Amber turning cloudy with water; star anise, liquorice, fennel and herbs
Pastis; Bardouin lists its herbs on the back
Un Bardouin, or un pastis. Names: Henri Bardouin (Distilleries et Domaines de Provence, Forcalquier); Ricard and Pastis 51 (Marseille)

bars:La Grange à Vins.name: La Grange à Vins
bars:La Grange à Vins.teaser: A Louis XV sommelier, 30 wines by the glass and a village cellar in La Croix-Valmer
bars:La Grange à Vins.story: La Grange is a wine shop and bar on La Croix-Valmer's main street, twelve minutes from Cavalaire. It was taken over in 2019 by Eric Brunet and the sommelier Mickaël Zortian, who worked at Alain Ducasse's Louis XV in Monaco. Around 30 wines are open by the glass from several hundred references, running from classic estates to natural bottles, with an armagnac shelf as well. Boards of charcuterie and cheese and a few homemade dishes come with them, and musicians play some summer evenings. The natural-wine app Raisin lists it.
bars:La Grange à Vins.why: Ask Zortian for a living wine by the glass, not the safe rosé.

bars:HERA.name: HERA, Saint-Tropez
bars:HERA.teaser: A small bistro-bar on the quai de l'Épi, run by a Vague d'Or alumna and open all year
bars:HERA.story: HERA is a small bistro and wine bar on the quai de l'Épi in Saint-Tropez, with tables outside by the harbour. Marylou Contreras, who worked front of house at La Vague d'Or, took over a little wine bar and turned it into a bistro; the kitchen was led in 2023 by Florent Manini and Anna Thillaye, both from Cheval Blanc St-Tropez. The cooking is seasonal and mostly organic, and the wine list puts classic, organic and natural bottles side by side. The critic Gilles Pudlowski called it the good surprise of Saint-Tropez.

bars:Fondugues-Pradugues.name: Fondugues-Pradugues
bars:Fondugues-Pradugues.teaser: Biodynamic wine by the glass under umbrella pines, with tapas from a truck and a pétanque pitch
bars:Fondugues-Pradugues.story: Fondugues-Pradugues is a biodynamic estate of about 14 hectares on the route des Plages at Ramatuelle, certified organic and Demeter. The vines are picked by hand, the ferments start on their own yeasts, and sulphur is kept low. In summer the estate sets out tables under the parasol pines, where L'Éphémère, a wine truck, pours its wines by the glass with tapas and there is a pétanque pitch beside them. It is the gulf's clearest look at living wine made on the spot rather than shipped in.
bars:Fondugues-Pradugues.why: Taste the reds as well as the rosé: low sulphur shows most in them.

bars:Bar 1904, La Messardière.name: Bar 1904, La Messardière
bars:Bar 1904, La Messardière.teaser: A Belle Époque château bar above Saint-Tropez bay: one cocktail, with the palace prices that come with it
bars:Bar 1904, La Messardière.story: La Messardière is a turreted château in its own park on the hill above Saint-Tropez, given as a wedding present by the cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise. The house names its bar for 1904, when, it says, Madame de La Messardière began serving refreshments to her guests, which it counts among the first bars on the Côte d'Azur. Airelles restored the château and reopened it as a palace hotel in July 2021. Bar 1904 is a shaded terrace by day and a low-lit room after dark. Prices are palace prices: one drink, not an evening.
bars:Bar 1904, La Messardière.why: Take one drink on the terrace at the end of the afternoon, with the bay below.

bars:Bar de La Ménado.name: Bar de La Ménado
bars:Bar de La Ménado.teaser: Twenty metres from the sand, a hotel terrace with a barman, a low sun and no DJ
bars:Bar de La Ménado.story: La Ménado is a four-star hotel on allée de la Plage, twenty metres from Cavalaire's beach, and its outdoor bar is the calm end of the town's evening. Classic and house cocktails come with sharing platters after dark. There is no band, no DJ and no dance floor, just the terrace, the water and the light going down over Cap Cavalaire. That is the attraction. It is strictly a high-summer bar, open only from mid-June to mid-September, so by October the terrace is shut.

bars:La Rhumerie.name: La Rhumerie
bars:La Rhumerie.teaser: Rum cocktails over the moored boats, a dance floor the size of a dinghy, and bands until late
bars:La Rhumerie.story: After dark Cavalaire's energy gathers in the gap between the moored boats and the Nouveau Port quay, and La Rhumerie is where it ends up. A bamboo-and-timber terrace looks over the hulls; the drinks are rum cocktails, the food apéro boards, and on band or DJ nights a small dance floor fills. It is the nearest thing the town has to a club, and it is honestly a bar. Its real advantage is the calendar: it trades from February to November, so it is still open while most of the seafront has shut. For an actual nightclub you have to go to Saint-Tropez.
bars:La Rhumerie.why: Come late in the season, when it is one of the few lights still on along the port.

bars:Marina Viva Plage.name: Marina Viva Plage
bars:Marina Viva Plage.teaser: A beach bar on the sand where Cavalaire's two real party nights, 21 June and 14 July, happen
bars:Marina Viva Plage.story: Cavalaire's nightlife lives on the beach and on the calendar, not in a fixed club, and Marina Viva Plage shows how. It is a private-beach restaurant with a cocktail bar on the sand, its drinks devised by the barman Thomas and timed to sunset. On the two nights the town properly goes out, the Fête de la Musique on 21 June and Bastille Day on 14 July, the venue throws an evening of its own, tapas and rosé for the music and the fireworks over the bay for the fourteenth. Any other night the bar winds down around 19:00.

bars:Playa Mezcala.name: Playa Mezcala
bars:Playa Mezcala.teaser: Feet in the sand at the Pardigon end of Cavalaire's bay, with ceviche, tacos and a mezcal at golden hour
bars:Playa Mezcala.story: Playa Mezcala is a beach club at the eastern, Pardigon end of Cavalaire's own bay, towards La Croix-Valmer and close to the landing beach. Its address, on avenue de Saint-Raphaël, is just the coast road's name. The style is a Mexican cantina on Var sand, mezcal included, and the kitchen mixes Mediterranean cooking with Latin American dishes: ceviche, tacos, empanadas, nachos, and a fish of the day. Sunbeds and a bar run through the day. Outside high summer it is a place for an apéritif at sunset, not a late night.
